summary: Describes SOCKS version 5, a protocol that lets a client connect through a firewall or proxy server. It supports pluggable authentication and is an evolution of version 4. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A friendly doorman who makes calls for you from inside a building. You tell him who you want to reach, and he connects you if you are allowed.

what is udp associate in socks
subtitle: A general framework that lets TCP and UDP applications pass through a firewall via a SOCKS server, with pluggable authentication.

tldr.problem: Firewalls isolate an internal network, and applications need a general, authenticated way to traverse them rather than relying on per-protocol gateways.
tldr.mechanism: The client opens a TCP connection to the SOCKS server, negotiates an authentication method, then sends a CONNECT, BIND or UDP ASSOCIATE request and gets back a reply with a bound address and port.
tldr.outcome: Version 5 extends SOCKS version 4 with UDP support, strong authentication methods and domain-name and IPv6 addressing.

today: RFC 1928 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text defers the method-specific sub-negotiations to separate memos.

sections.title: Why SOCKS Exists
sections.content:
Network firewalls isolate an organization's internal network from an outside network such as the Internet. They typically act as application-layer gateways offering controlled TELNET, FTP and SMTP access. As more sophisticated application protocols appeared, a general framework was needed for them to traverse a firewall transparently and securely, with strong authentication as fine-grained as practical.

SOCKS version 5 is conceptually a shim layer between the application layer and the transport layer. For that reason it does not provide network-layer gateway services such as forwarding ICMP messages.

It evolves SOCKS version 4, which gave unsecured firewall traversal for TCP applications. Version 5 adds UDP, a framework for generalized strong authentication, and addressing by domain name and IPv6 address. Using SOCKS typically means recompiling or relinking TCP client applications with a SOCKS library.
sections.eli5: A company keeps its computers behind a wall. SOCKS is the single gate in that wall, and it checks who you are before it lets your messages through.

sections.title: Connecting and Choosing Authentication
sections.content:
A TCP client that needs to reach something only reachable through the firewall opens a TCP connection to the SOCKS server, conventionally on TCP port 1080. It then negotiates an authentication method, authenticates, and sends a relay request. The server either sets up the connection or denies it.

The client first sends a version identifier and method selection message: a VER octet (X'05'), an NMETHODS octet and one to 255 method octets. The server picks one and replies with VER and METHOD. If the chosen method is X'FF', none of the offered methods is acceptable and the client MUST close the connection.

Compliant implementations MUST support GSSAPI and SHOULD support USERNAME/PASSWORD. After selection, the client and server run a method-specific sub-negotiation, described in separate memos. If the method provides encapsulation for integrity or confidentiality, later requests and replies MUST use it.
sections.eli5: First you knock and say which ways you can prove who you are, such as a password. The doorman picks one, or tells you none of them is good enough and you must leave.

sections.title: Requests and Addresses
sections.content:
Once authentication is done, the client sends a request: VER, CMD, a reserved octet X'00', ATYP, DST.ADDR and a two-octet DST.PORT in network octet order. There are three commands.

  • CONNECT (X'01') asks the server to connect to the destination.
  • BIND (X'02') is for protocols where the client must accept a connection from the server. FTP is the example, with data transfers coming back from server to client. It is expected to be used only for secondary connections after a primary one is set up with CONNECT.
  • UDP ASSOCIATE (X'03') sets up a UDP relay association.

The ATYP field says what kind of address follows: X'01' is an IPv4 address of 4 octets, X'04' is an IPv6 address of 16 octets, and X'03' is a fully-qualified domain name whose first octet gives the number of name octets that follow, with no terminating NUL.

The server typically evaluates the request using the source and destination addresses.
sections.eli5: After you are let in, you tell the doorman what you want: call this address, wait here for someone to call me, or pass along some quick postcards. You can name the place by number or by its name.

sections.title: Replies and Command Behaviour
sections.content:
The server answers with VER, REP, a reserved octet, ATYP, BND.ADDR and BND.PORT. REP of X'00' means success; other values name the failure. Reserved fields are set to X'00'.

For CONNECT, the bound address and port are what the server assigned to connect to the target. This address often differs from the one the client used to reach the server, since such servers are often multi-homed.

For BIND, the server sends two replies. The first comes after it creates and binds a socket and gives the address and port it is listening on, which the client typically passes to the application server over the primary connection. The second comes after the incoming connection succeeds or fails and carries the address and port of the connecting host.

For UDP ASSOCIATE, DST.ADDR and DST.PORT say where the client expects to send UDP from; if it does not know yet it MUST use all zeros. The reply's bound address and port say where the client MUST send UDP messages to be relayed. The association ends when the TCP connection that carried the request ends.

When a reply signals failure, the server MUST terminate the TCP connection shortly after, no more than 10 seconds after detecting the cause. After a successful CONNECT or BIND the client may pass data, using method-dependent encapsulation if the method has any.
sections.eli5: The doorman tells you whether it worked, and if not, why: the line was busy, the place does not exist, or the rules say no. If he says no, he hangs up soon after.

sections.title: Relaying UDP Datagrams
sections.content:
A UDP client MUST send its datagrams to the UDP port given in BND.PORT of the UDP ASSOCIATE reply, wrapped in any method-dependent encapsulation. Each datagram carries a UDP request header: a two-octet reserved field X'0000', a one-octet FRAG, ATYP, DST.ADDR, DST.PORT and then the data.

The relay forwards datagrams silently, with no notice to the client, and drops those it cannot or will not relay. Replies from remote hosts are wrapped in the same header. The relay MUST learn from the SOCKS server the expected client IP address for the association and MUST drop datagrams from any other source address.

Fragmentation is optional. In FRAG, the high-order bit marks the end of a fragment sequence, X'00' means a standalone datagram, and values 1 to 127 give the position. Receivers keep a reassembly queue and timer, and the timer MUST be no less than 5 seconds. An implementation without fragmentation MUST drop any datagram whose FRAG is not X'00'. Applications are advised to avoid fragmentation.

A SOCKS-aware UDP interface MUST report available buffer space smaller than the real space: by 10 octets plus method overhead for IPv4, 262 for domain names and 20 for IPv6.
sections.eli5: For quick postcards, you hand them to a special mailbox the doorman names. He forwards them and brings back replies, but he only accepts mail from the person he expects.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security of firewall traversal with SOCKS depends heavily on the authentication and encapsulation methods an implementation offers and those chosen during negotiation. The RFC adds only that administrators should consider the choice of authentication methods carefully.
sections.eli5: How safe the gate is depends on how good the ID check is, so the people running it should pick the check carefully.
